title: Rantideva's last cup: whose is wealth?
hook: a starving king gives his last food and water to guests, and the Isha's first verse asks whose wealth it is anyway
carry: it's all the lord's: enjoy it, don't grab
tomorrow: Arjuna drops his bow: work that doesn't cling

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, and the lingam, a sign of what has no end. Now the festivals are done, and three days begin on karma, the way of action.
screen: `A SIGN OF WHAT HAS NO END.`

segments.voice: A king hasn't eaten in forty-eight days. Not for a vow: he has given everything away, and his family has gone hungry with him. On the forty-ninth morning, food and water arrive. He's about to eat when there's a knock. A guest. Then another. Then another. A short Upanishad asks the question his story answers: whose, after all, is anything you own?
screen: `FORTY-EIGHT DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` → `A MEAL ARRIVES.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its ninth book. King Rantideva sees the Lord in every being, so he gives a share to the first guest, a brahmin. Then a laborer comes, and he gives again. Then a man with a pack of hungry dogs, and he gives the rest of the food. Only the water is left, and an outcaste comes begging for a drink. Rantideva is dying of thirst himself. He gives it, and says, roughly: I don't ask for powers, or even for freedom from rebirth; let me take on the pain of every being, so they're free of it. Then the guests show themselves: they were the gods, come to test him. He asks them for nothing. Now hear the Isha Upanishad's first verse beside him. Isha vasyam idam sarvam: all this, whatever moves in this moving world, is dwelt in by the Lord. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: enjoy by letting go, or, in another reading, enjoy what has been given. Ma gridhah: do not covet. Kasya svid dhanam: whose, after all, is wealth? That's the Hindu teaching under karma, the way of action: what you have isn't finally yours. It's the Lord's, lent to you. Shankara hears renunciation in the verse; others hear gratitude. Rantideva is the extreme case. The everyday case is in many Hindu kitchens: food is offered to God first, and only then eaten, as prasad, a gift given back. Gandhi is reported to have said that if every other scripture were lost and only this verse survived, Hinduism would still live.
screen: `RANTIDEVA GIVES TO EVERY GUEST.` · `HIS LAST WATER, TO AN OUTCASTE.` · `ALL THIS IS DWELT IN BY THE LORD.` · `DON'T COVET. WHOSE IS WEALTH?` · then, large: `IT'S ALL THE LORD'S: ENJOY, DON'T GRAB.`

segments.voice: At your next meal, do what many Hindu homes do: pause with the plate before you eat. If you pray, offer it silently to God, in any words. If you don't, think of everyone and everything that made it. Either way, say to yourself the verse's question, whose is this, really? Then eat it slowly, as a gift.
Karma. Action, from the root kri, to do. The Isha says act and enjoy in a world that belongs to the Lord, not to you.
Your line: it's all the Lord's: enjoy it, don't grab. Tomorrow, a warrior who wants to quit. Day six hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes offer food to God before anyone eats and receive it back as prasad; teachers of karma yoga often cite the Isha's first verse for the same posture in working life: act and enjoy without the sense of owning.
